title: Could Minnesota spoil the blue wave?
contentHtml:
Although our critics might disagree, we seek to avoid false equivocation at Silver Bulletin. Generally, when a party is ahead in our forecast, we’ll highlight why our model thinks they’re winning. Democrats have the better hand to play in the Senate; that’s been clear for a couple of weeks now. At the same time, we try to cover our bases. FLIPR’s forecasts are probabilistic, and we feel a duty to explain the downside and upside scenarios. There remains a very real chance — about 1 in 4 — that Republicans keep the Senate despite Democrats’ seeming momentum. And they have two basic ways they can do that: by holding Democrats to fewer than the four pickups they need, or by “stealing” one or more currently D-held seats.

Alternatively, Democrats could still win the Senate even if they do lose some of their own seats by flipping more than four GOP-held states.

Senate seats used to flip in both directions in the midterms. The 1978 election was the most absurd example: Republicans picked up eight Senate seats from Democrats (dark red) while Democrats flipped five seats to their side (dark blue). Net gain: GOP +3. Not a bad night, but Democrats retained a clear majority.

However, in the past five midterms, a “double flip” has happened only once, in 2018. On the surface, that looks like a really weird result. Democrats won the popular vote for the U.S. House by more than 8 points, flipping dozens of seats in the process. They also flipped GOP Senate seats in Arizona and Nevada. But they lost four Senate seats of their own: North Dakota, Missouri, Indiana and Florida. Net result: +41 House seats, but -2 in the Senate.

This seeming weirdness, though, was well predicted by models. Senators serve six-year terms, of course, and that’s an eternity in politics. The senators up for re-election in 2018 were from the class of 2012, a strong year for Democrats. Their terms straddled the election of Donald Trump, whose win signaled increasing political polarization and more specifically, a growing divide between college-educated voters in the cities and white working-class voters in the rural heartland. Indiana, North Dakota and Missouri fit the pattern, with the red shift among rural whites outweighing the strongly blue background environment. Florida didn’t so much, but Bill Nelson’s loss there marked the beginning of a death spiral for Democrats in the state.

I won’t spend much more time on why “double flips” are becoming less common because you probably know the story. Perpetually increasing polarization means that: 1) fewer states are competitive; 2) there’s less and less ticket-splitting, so races for Congress are more predictable based on presidential voting and 3) “candidate effects,” including incumbency, are weaker, so there’s less opportunity for a candidate with strong personal qualities to overcome the partisan tide.

Instead, let’s focus on these questions: 1) What is the chance of a “double flip” happening this year in the Senate, with both parties picking up at least one seat? 2) How screwed are Democrats if this happens: could they plausibly lose one of their own seats and still take over the Senate? 3) What should we think about Minnesota in particular, where Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is in a surprisingly close race in polls against former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya?

A double flip is plausible this year, but not a good bet at even money

This part of the equation is easy: Democrats are extremely likely to pick up at least one currently Republican-held seat.
